meta.negative_marking_rule: One-third of the marks assigned to the question is deducted for each wrong answer; no penalty for unattempted questions.
meta.answer_key_source: Official UPSC Answer Key & standard analytical solutions.

passages.title: Demographic Growth and Agrarian Dependence in India
passages.text: Global population was around 1.6 billion in 1990 — today it is around 7.2 billion and growing. Recent estimates on population growth predict a global population of 9.6 billion in 2050 and 10.9 billion in 2100. Unlike Europe and North America, where only three to four per cent of population is engaged in agriculture, around 47 per cent of India's population is dependent upon agriculture. Even if India continues to do well in the service sector and the manufacturing sector picks up, it is expected that around 2030 when India overtakes China as the world's most populous country, nearly 42 per cent of India's population will still be predominantly dependent on agriculture.

passages.title: Globalization of Food Production and Foodborne Pathogens
passages.text: Many pathogens that cause foodborne illnesses are unknown. Food contamination can occur at any stage from farm to plate. Since most cases of food poisoning go unreported, the true extent of global foodborne illnesses is unknown. Improvements in international monitoring have led to greater public awareness, yet the rapid globalization of food production increases consumers' vulnerability by making food harder to regulate and trace. "We have the world on our plates", says an official of WHO.

passages.title: Science, Faith, and Existential Inquiry
passages.text: I am a scientist, privileged to be somebody who tries to understand nature using the tools of science. But it is also clear that there are some really important questions that science cannot really answer, such as: Why is there something instead of nothing? Why are we here? In those domains, I have found that faith provides a better path to answers. I find it oddly anachronistic that in today's culture there seems to be a widespread presumption that scientific and spiritual views are incompatible.

passages.title: Tradition, Freedom, and Historical Inheritance
passages.text: Though I have discarded much of past tradition and custom, and am anxious that India should rid herself of all shackles that bind and contain her and divide her people, and suppress vast numbers of them, and prevent the free development of the body and the spirit; though I seek all this, yet I do not wish to cut myself off from that past completely. I am proud of that great inheritance that has been and is, ours and I am conscious that I too, like all of us, am a link in that unbroken chain which goes back to the dawn of history in the immemorial past of India.

passages.title: Universal Access, School Mapping, and Quality in Education
passages.text: It is no longer enough for us to talk about providing for universal access to education. Making available schooling facilities is an essential prerequisite, but is insufficient to ensure that all children attend school and participate in the learning process. The school may be there, but children may not attend or they may drop out after a few months. Through school and social mapping, we must address the entire gamut of social, economic, cultural and indeed linguistic and pedagogic issues, factors that prevent children from weaker sections and disadvantaged groups, as also girls, from regularly attending and complementing elementary education. The focus must be on the poorest and most vulnerable since these groups are the most disempowered and at the greatest risk of violation or denial of their right to education. The right to education goes beyond free and compulsory education to include quality education for all. Quality is an integral part of the right to education. If the education process lacks quality, children are being denied their right. The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act lays down that the curriculum should provide for learning through activities, exploration and discovery. This places an obligation on us to change our perception of children as passive receivers of knowledge, and to move beyond the convention of using textbooks as the basis of examinations. The teaching-learning process must become stress-free; and a massive programme for curricular reform should be initiated to provide for a child-friendly learning system, that is more relevant and empowering. Teacher accountability systems and processes must ensure that children are learning, and that their right to learn in a child-friendly environment is not violated. Testing and assessment systems must be reexamined and redesigned to ensure that these do not force children to struggle between school and tuition centres, and bypass childhood.

passages.title: Desertification, Deforestation, and Watershed Degradation
passages.text: 'Desertification' is a term used to explain a process of decline in the biological productivity of an ecosystem, leading to total loss of productivity. While this phenomenon is often linked to the arid, semi-arid and sub-humid ecosystems, even in the humid tropics, the impact could be most dramatic. Impoverishment of human-impacted terrestrial ecosystems may exhibit itself in a variety of ways: accelerated erosion as in the mountain regions of the country, salinization of land as in the semi-arid and arid 'green revolution' areas of the country, e.g., Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, and site quality decline — a common phenomenon due to general decline in tree cover and monotonous monoculture of rice/wheat across the Indian plains. A major consequence of deforestation is that it relates to adverse alterations in the hydrology and related soil and nutrient losses. The consequences of deforestation invariably arise out of site degradation through erosive losses. Tropical Asia, Africa and South America have the highest levels of erosion. The already high rates for the tropics are increasing at an alarming rate (e.g., through the major river systems — Ganga and Brahmaputra, in the Indian context), due to deforestation and ill-suited land management practices subsequent to forest clearing. In the mountain context, the declining moisture retention of the mountain soils, drying up of the underground springs and smaller rivers in the Himalayan region could be attributed to drastic changes in the forest cover. An indirect consequence is drastic alteration in the upland-lowland interaction, mediated through water. The current concern the tea planter of Assam has is about the damage to tea plantations due to frequent inundation along the flood-plains of Brahmaputra, and the damage to tea plantation and the consequent loss in tea productivity is due to rising level of the river bottom because of siltation and the changing course of the river system. The ultimate consequences of site desertification are soil degradation, alteration in available water and its quality, and the consequent decline in food, fodder and fuel-wood yields essential for the economic well-being of rural communities.

passages.title: Natural Asset Diversity and Proactive Adaptation to Climate Change
passages.text: A diversity of natural assets will be needed to cope with climate change and ensure productive agriculture, forestry, and fisheries. For example, crop varieties are needed that perform well under drought, heat, and enhanced CO2. But the private-sector and farmer-led process of choosing crops favours homogeneity adapted to past or current conditions, not varieties capable of producing consistently high yields in warmer, wetter, or drier conditions. Accelerated breeding programmes are needed to conserve a wider pool of genetic resources of existing crops, breeds, and their wild relatives. Relatively intact ecosystems, such as forested catchments, mangroves, wetlands, can buffer the impacts of climate change. Under a changing climate, these ecosystems are themselves at risk, and management approaches will need to be more proactive and adaptive. Connections between natural areas, such as migration corridors, may be needed to facilitate species movements to keep up with the change in climate.

passages.title: Human Aspirations and Earth as a Biological System
passages.text: Today, the top environmental challenge is a combination of people and their aspirations. If the aspirations are more like the frugal ones we had after the Second World War, a lot more is possible than if we view the planet as a giant shopping mall. We need to get beyond the fascination with glitter and understand that the planet works as a biological system.

passages.title: Leadership as a Teachable, Acquired Art
passages.text: Some people believe that leadership is a quality which you have at birth or not at all. This theory is false, for the art of leadership can be acquired and can indeed be taught. This discovery is made in time of war and the results achieved can surprise even the instructors. Faced with the alternatives of going left or right, every soldier soon grasps that a prompt decision either way is better than an endless discussion. A firm choice of direction has an even chance of being right while to do nothing will be almost certainly wrong.

passages.title: Financing Climate Adaptation and Mitigation in Developing Nations
passages.text: All actions to address climate change ultimately involve costs. Funding is vital in order for countries like India to design and implement adaptation and mitigation plans and projects. The problem is more severe for developing countries like India, which would be one of the hardest hit by climate change, given its need to finance development. Most countries do indeed treat climate change as real threat and are striving to address it in a more comprehensive and integrated manner with the limited resources at their disposal.

passages.title: Indoor Air Pollution and Clean Cooking Energy
passages.text: Cooking with biomass and coal in India is now recognized to cause major health problems, with women and children in poor populations facing the greatest risk. There are more than 10 lakh premature deaths each year from household air pollution due to polluting cooking fuels with another 1.5 lakh due to their contribution to general outdoor air pollution in the country. Although the fraction of the Indian population using clean cooking fuels, such as LPG, natural gas and electricity, is slowly rising, the number using polluting solid fuels as their primary cooking fuel has remained static for nearly 30 years at about 70 crore.

passages.title: Science as Liberator and Architect of a Better World
passages.text: Scientific knowledge has its dangers, but so has every great thing. Over and beyond the dangers with which it threatens the present, it opens up as nothing else can, the vision of a possible happy world; a world without poverty, without war, with little illness. Science, whatever unpleasant consequences it may have by the way, is in its very nature a liberator.

passages.title: Resource Scramble in the Melting Arctic
passages.text: The Arctic's vast reserves of fossil fuel, fish and minerals are now accessible for a longer period in a year. But unlike Antarctica, which is protected from exploitation by the Antarctic Treaty framed during the Cold War and is not subject to territorial claims by any country, there is no legal regime protecting the Arctic from industrialization, especially at a time when the world craves for more and more resources. The distinct possibility of ice-free summer has prompted countries with Arctic coastline to scramble for great chunks of the melting ocean.

passages.title: WTO Agriculture Agreement and Domestic Food Security
passages.text: Being a member of the WTO, India is bound by the agreements that have been signed and ratified by its members, including itself. According to Article 6 of the Agriculture Agreement, providing minimum support prices for agricultural products is considered distorting and is subject to limits. The subsidy arising from 'minimal supports' cannot exceed 10 per cent of the value of agricultural production for developing countries. PDS in India entails minimum support prices and public stockholding of food grains. It is possible that, in some years, the subsidy to producers will exceed 10 per cent of the value of agricultural production.

passages.title: 19th-Century Industrial Schooling vs. Complex 21st-Century Economy
passages.text: India's educational system is modelled on the mass education system that developed in the 19th century in Europe and later spread around the world. The goal of the system is to condition children as 'good' citizens and productive workers. This suited the industrial age that needed the constant supply of a compliant workforce with a narrow set of capabilities. Our educational institutes resemble factories with bells, uniforms and batch-processing of learners, designed to get learners to conform. But, from an economic point of view, the environment today is very different. It is a complex, volatile and globally interconnected world.

passages.title: Individual Biochemical Individuality and the Failure of Diets
passages.text: The practice of dieting has become an epidemic; everyone is looking out for a way to attain that perfect body. We are all different with respect to our ethnicity, genetics, family history, gender, age, physical and mental and spiritual health status, lifestyles and preferences. Thereby we also differ in what foods we tolerate or are sensitive to. So we really cannot reduce so many complexities into one diet or diet book. This explains the failure of diets across the world in curbing obesity. Unless the reasons for weight gain are well understood and addressed and unless habits are changed permanently, no diet is likely to succeed.

passages.title: Monoculture Vulnerability in an Era of Climate Extremes
passages.text: Monoculture carries great risks. A single disease or pest can wipe out swathes of the world's food production, an alarming prospect given that its growing and wealthier population will eat 70% more by 2050. The risks are magnified by the changing climate. As the planet warms and monsoon rains intensify, farmlands in Asia will flood. North America will suffer more intense droughts, and crop diseases will spread to new latitudes.

passages.title: Industrial Factory Farming and Animal Pandemics
passages.text: The quest for cheap and plentiful meat has resulted in factory farms where more and more animals are squeezed into smaller lots in cruel and shocking conditions. Such practices have resulted in many of the world's health pandemics such as the avian flu. Worldwide, livestock are increasingly raised in cruel, cramped conditions, where animals spend their short lives under artificial light, pumped full of antibiotics and growth hormones, until the day they are slaughtered. Meat production is water-intensive — 15000 litres of water is needed for every kilogram of meat compared with 3400 litres for rice, 3300 litres for eggs and 255 litres for a kilogram of potatoes.

passages.title: Tiger Dispersal, Habitat Fragmentation, and Corridors
passages.text: A male tiger was removed from Pench Tiger Reserve and was relocated in Panna National Park. Later, this tiger trekked toward his home 250 miles away. The trek of this solitary tiger highlights a crisis. Many wildlife reserves exist as islands of fragile habitat in a vast sea of humanity, yet tigers can range over a hundred miles, seeking prey, mates and territory. Nearly a third of India's tigers live outside tiger reserves, a situation that is dangerous for both human and animal. Prey and tigers can only disperse if there are recognized corridors of land between protected areas to allow unmolested passage.

questions.question:
Consider the following three-dimensional figure:
[A regular icosahedron solid]
How many triangles does the above figure have?
questions.explanation: The given three-dimensional geometric figure is a regular icosahedron, one of the five Platonic solids. A regular icosahedron has exactly 20 equilateral triangular faces, 12 vertices, and 30 edges. Therefore, the figure has 20 triangles.

questions.question:
Consider the following sum:
• + 1• + 2• + •3 + •1 = 21•
In the above sum, • stands for
questions.explanation:
Let • represent the single digit d. Express the equation in place values:
d + (10 + d) + (20 + d) + (10d + 3) + (10d + 1) = 200 + 10 + d
LHS = d + 10 + d + 20 + d + 10d + 3 + 10d + 1 = 34 + 23d.
RHS = 210 + d.
Equating LHS and RHS: 34 + 23d = 210 + d => 22d = 176 => d = 176 / 22 = 8.
Therefore, • stands for 8.

questions.question:
Consider the following pattern of numbers:
Row 1: 8 | 10 | 15 | 13
Row 2: 6 | 5 | 7 | 4
Row 3: 4 | 6 | 8 | 8
Row 4: 6 | 11 | 16 | ?
What is the number at ? in the above pattern?
questions.explanation: Look at each column: Col 1: (8 + 4) - 6 = 6; Col 2: (10 + 6) - 5 = 11; Col 3: (15 + 8) - 7 = 16. In general, for each column: (Row 1 + Row 3) - Row 2 = Row 4. For Column 4: (13 + 8) - 4 = 21 - 4 = 17. Thus, ? = 17.

questions.question: How many diagonals can be drawn by joining the vertices of an octagon?
questions.explanation: The number of diagonals of an n-sided polygon is given by n(n - 3) / 2. For an octagon, n = 8. Number of diagonals = 8 × (8 - 3) / 2 = 8 × 5 / 2 = 20.

questions.question: The figure drawn gives the velocity graphs of two vehicles A and B. The straight line OKP represents the velocity of vehicle A at any instant, whereas the horizontal straight line CKD represents the velocity of vehicle B at any instant. In the figure, D is the point where perpendicular from P meets the horizontal line CKD such that PD = ½ LD. What is the ratio between the distances covered by vehicles A and B in the time interval OL?
questions.explanation:
The distance covered by a vehicle is represented by the area under its velocity-time curve over the time interval OL.
Let time OL = t.
For vehicle B, the velocity is constant: v_B = OC = LD = h.
Distance covered by vehicle B = Area of rectangle OCKDL = OL × LD = t × h.
For vehicle A, the velocity starts from 0 at O and increases linearly to PL at time L.
We are given PD = ½ LD = ½ h. Therefore, total height PL = LD + PD = h + ½ h = 1.5h.
Distance covered by vehicle A = Area of triangle OPL = ½ × Base × Height = ½ × t × (1.5h) = 0.75 th = ¾ th.
Ratio of distances covered by vehicle A to vehicle B = (¾ th) / (th) = 3/4 = 3:4.

questions.question: A train 200 metres long is moving at the rate of 40 kmph. In how many seconds will it cross a man standing near the railway line?
questions.explanation:
Speed of train = 40 km/h = 40 × (5/18) m/s = 200 / 18 = 100 / 9 m/s.
Distance to be covered to cross a standing man = Length of the train = 200 m.
Time taken = Distance / Speed = 200 / (200/18) = 18 seconds.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most logical and rational inference that can be made from the above passage?

options.text: Prosperity of agriculture sector is of critical importance to India.
Indian economy greatly depends on its agriculture.
India should take strict measures to control its rapid population growth.
India's farming communities should switch over to other occupations to improve their economic conditions.

questions.explanation: The passage highlights that around 47% of India's population depends on agriculture, and even by 2030, nearly 42% will remain dependent on it despite growth in services and manufacturing, logically inferring that the prosperity of the agricultural sector is of critical importance to India.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most logical corollary to the above passage?

options.text: With more options for food come more risks.
Food processing is the source of all foodborne illnesses.
We should depend on locally produced food only.
Globalization of food production should be curtailed.

questions.explanation: The passage notes that rapid globalization of food production puts 'the world on our plates', making food harder to regulate and trace, and increasing consumer vulnerability to foodborne pathogens, yielding the logical corollary that with more global food options come more risks.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most logical and rational inference that can be made from the above passage?

options.text: It is the faith and not science that can finally solve all the problems of mankind.
Science and faith can be mutually complementary if their proper domains are understood.
There are some very fundamental questions which cannot be answered by either science or faith.
In today's culture, scientific views are given more importance than spiritual views.

questions.explanation: The author (Dr. Francis Collins) explains that science uses tools to understand the physical mechanisms of nature while faith addresses existential questions (why we are here), concluding that viewing science and faith as incompatible is anachronistic, inferring that they are mutually complementary within their respective domains.

questions.question: The author wants India to rid herself of certain past bonds because

options.text: he is not able to see the relevance of the past
there is not much to be proud of
he is not interested in the history of India
they obstruct her physical and spiritual growth

questions.explanation: Jawaharlal Nehru writes in The Discovery of India that he wants India to rid herself of those shackles of the past because they 'bind and contain her and divide her people, and suppress vast numbers of them, and prevent the free development of the body and the spirit'.

questions.question: By how much (measured in thousands of tons) did the import of sheet steel exceed the import of coil steel in the first three months of the year?
questions.explanation:
From the bar chart for the first three months (January, February, March):
- Sheet steel imports: Jan = 40, Feb = 37, Mar = 36. Total sheet steel = 40 + 37 + 36 = 113 thousand tons.
- Coil steel imports: Jan = 30, Feb = 31, Mar = 33. Total coil steel = 30 + 31 + 33 = 94 thousand tons.
Difference = 113 − 94 = 19 thousand tons.

questions.question: What was the approximate total value (in $) of sheet steel imported over the six months period?
questions.explanation:
Total sheet steel imported over the six months (in thousand tons):
Jan(40) + Feb(37) + Mar(36) + Apr(36) + May(34) + Jun(34) = 217 thousand tons = 217,000 tons.
Average cost per ton of sheet steel = $256.
Total value = 217,000 × $256 = $55,552,000 (which corresponds to 55,550 in thousands of dollars).

questions.question: What was the approximate ratio of sheet steel and scrap steel imports in the first three months of the year?
questions.explanation:
In the first three months (Jan, Feb, Mar):
- Sheet steel = 40 + 37 + 36 = 113 thousand tons.
- Scrap steel = Jan(32) + Feb(34) + Mar(32) = 98 thousand tons.
Ratio = 113 / 98 ≈ 1.153 : 1 ≈ 1.2:1.

questions.question: Rotated positions of a single solid are shown. The various faces of the solid are marked with different symbols like dots, cross and line. What is the symbol on the face opposite to that containing a single dot?
questions.explanation:
Analyzing the adjacent faces of the solid across orientations (I) to (IV):
- From figures (I) and (II), the face with a single dot is adjacent to two dots, four dots, cross, and line.
- The only face not adjacent to the single dot is the face with three dots.
Therefore, the face containing three dots is opposite to the single dot.

questions.question: What is the symbol on the face opposite to that containing two dots?
questions.explanation:
Opposite pairs on the solid are:
- Single dot is opposite to Three dots.
- Two dots is opposite to Four dots.
- Cross is opposite to Line.
Therefore, the symbol on the face opposite to two dots is Four dots.

questions.question: What is the symbol on the face opposite to that containing the cross?
questions.explanation:
From the deduced opposite pairs:
- Single dot is opposite to Three dots.
- Two dots is opposite to Four dots.
- Cross is opposite to Line.
Therefore, the symbol on the face opposite to the cross is the Line.

questions.question:
According to the passage, which of the following is/are of paramount importance under the Right to Education?
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
statements: 1. Sending of children to school by all parents
2. Provision of adequate physical infrastructure in schools
3. Curricular reforms for developing child-friendly learning system
questions.explanation: The passage argues that universal physical access and infrastructure are merely prerequisites, and that 'Quality is an integral part of the right to education... a massive programme for curricular reform should be initiated to provide for a child-friendly learning system', making curricular reform of paramount importance.

questions.question:
With reference to the above passage, the following assumptions have been made:
Which of the above assumptions is/are valid?
statements: 1. The Right to Education guarantees teachers' accountability for the learning process of children.
2. The Right to Education guarantees 100% enrolment of children in the schools.
3. The Right to Education intends to take full advantage of demographic dividend.
questions.explanation: Assumption 1 is valid: the passage states that 'Teacher accountability systems and processes must ensure that children are learning, and that their right to learn in a child-friendly environment is not violated.' Assumptions 2 and 3 are unsupported claims (100% enrolment is not guaranteed by law alone, and demographic dividend is unmentioned).

questions.question: According to the passage, which one of the following is critical in bringing quality in education?

options.text: Ensuring regular attendance of children as well as teachers in school
Giving pecuniary benefits to teachers to motivate them
Understanding the socio-cultural background of children
Inculcating learning through activities and discovery

questions.explanation: The text highlights that the Act lays down that 'the curriculum should provide for learning through activities, exploration and discovery', moving beyond passive memorization of textbooks to bring genuine quality to education.

questions.question: What is the essential message in this passage?

options.text: The Right to Education now is a Fundamental Right.
The Right to Education enables the children of poor and weaker sections of the society to attend schools.
The Right to Free and Compulsory Education should include quality education for all.
The Government as well as parents should ensure that all children attend schools.

questions.explanation: The core thesis of the passage is stated explicitly: 'The right to education goes beyond free and compulsory education to include quality education for all. Quality is an integral part of the right to education. If the education process lacks quality, children are being denied their right.'

questions.question: If LSJXVC is the code for MUMBAI, the code for DELHI is
questions.explanation: Look at the letter shifts from MUMBAI to LSJXVC: M(-1)->L, U(-2)->S, M(-3)->J, B(-4)->X, A(-5)->V, I(-6)->C. Applying the same -1, -2, -3, -4, -5 shifts to DELHI gives: D(-1)->C, E(-2)->C, L(-3)->I, H(-4)->D, I(-5)->D, resulting in CCIDD.

questions.question: If RAMON is written as 12345 and DINESH as 675849, then HAMAM will be written as
questions.explanation: Extract digits: R=1, A=2, M=3, O=4, N=5, D=6, I=7, E=8, S=4, H=9. For HAMAM: H=9, A=2, M=3, A=2, M=3 -> 92323.

questions.question: If X is between -3 and -1, and Y is between -1 and 1, then X² - Y² is in between which of the following?
questions.explanation: X ∈ (-3, -1) => X² ∈ (1, 9). Y ∈ (-1, 1) => Y² ∈ [0, 1). Then X² - Y² ranges between 1 - 1 = 0 and 9 - 1 = 8. (UPSC official key: c).

questions.question: X and Y are natural numbers other than 1, and Y is greater than X. Which of the following represents the largest number?
questions.explanation: For natural numbers X, Y >= 2 with Y > X: X/Y < 1, (X+Y)/XY < 1, Y/X < Y < XY. Thus XY is strictly the largest.

questions.question: The plan of an office block for six officers A, B, C, D, E and F is as follows: Both B and C occupy offices to the right of the corridor (as one enters the office block) and A occupies on the left of the corridor. E and F occupy offices on opposite sides of the corridor but their offices do not face each other. The offices of C and D face each other. E does not have a corner office. F's office is further down the corridor than A's, but on the same side. If E sits in his office and faces the corridor, whose office is to his left?
questions.explanation: On the left side: D (near), A (middle), F (far). On the right side: C (near, facing D), E (middle, not corner), B (far). When E sits in the middle right office facing the corridor, to E's left is C's office.

questions.question: Who is/are F's immediate neighbour/neighbours?
questions.explanation: On the left side of the corridor, the offices from front to back are D, A, F. F is at the end, so F's only adjacent immediate neighbour on the same side is A.

questions.question:
According to the passage, which of the following are the consequences of decline in forest cover?
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
statements: 1. Loss of topsoil
2. Loss of smaller rivers
3. Adverse effect on agricultural production
4. Declining of groundwater
questions.explanation: All four are explicitly cited in the text: accelerated erosion causing topsoil loss (1), drying up of underground springs and smaller rivers (2 and 4), and site degradation causing decline in food, fodder, and crop yields (3).

questions.question:
Which of the following is/are the correct inference/inferences that can be made from the passage?
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
statements: 1. Deforestation can cause changes in the course of rivers.
2. Salinization of land takes place due to human activities only.
3. Intense monoculture practice in plains is a major reason for desertification in Tropical Asia, Africa and South America.

options.text: None of the above is a correct inference

questions.explanation: Inference 1 is correct: the passage links siltation and silt-loading from deforestation directly to 'rising level of the river bottom because of siltation and the changing course of the river system'. Statements 2 and 3 contain unjustified extreme qualifiers ('human activities only', monoculture in plains causing desertification across three continents).

questions.question:
With reference to 'desertification', as described in the passage, the following assumptions have been made:
Which of the above assumptions is/are valid?
statements: 1. Desertification is a phenomenon in tropical areas only.
2. Deforestation invariably leads to floods and desertification.
questions.explanation: Both assumptions are invalid: desertification is associated with arid and sub-humid zones generally, not tropical areas only; and stating deforestation 'invariably leads to floods and desertification' is an absolute over-generalization.

questions.question:
With reference to the above passage, which of the following would assist us in coping with the climate change?
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
statements: 1. Conservation of natural water sources
2. Conservation of wider gene pool
3. Existing crop management practices
4. Migration corridors
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly recommends conserving natural water sources/intact catchments (1), conserving a wider gene pool through accelerated breeding (2), and establishing migration corridors to facilitate species movements (4). Existing crop practices are described as promoting narrow homogeneity.

questions.question:
With reference to the above passage, the following assumptions have been made:
Which of the above assumptions is/are valid?
statements: 1. Diversification of livelihoods acts as a coping strategy for climate change.
2. Adoption of monocropping practice leads to the extinction of plant varieties and their wild relatives.
questions.explanation: Neither assumption is made by the author: livelihood diversification is not discussed, and the passage states monocropping favours homogeneity adapted to current conditions rather than asserting that it causes the extinction of wild relatives.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most crucial and logical inference that can be made from the above passage?

options.text: The Earth can meet only the basic needs of humans for food, clothing and shelter.
The only way to meet environmental challenge is to limit human population.
Reducing our consumerism is very much in our own interest.
Knowledge of biological systems can only help us save this planet.

questions.explanation: The author contrasts treating the planet as a giant shopping mall with embracing frugal aspirations and understanding that the Earth works as a biological system, logically inferring that reducing consumerism is essential and in our own self-interest.

questions.question: The author of the passage holds the view that

options.text: leadership can be taught through war experience only
leadership can be acquired as well as taught
the results of training show that more people acquire leadership than are expected
despite rigorous instruction, very few leaders are produced

questions.explanation: The author writes: 'the art of leadership can be acquired and can indeed be taught', which matches option (b) verbatim.

questions.question: A number consists of three digits of which the middle one is zero and their sum is 4. If the number formed by interchanging the first and last digits is greater than the number itself by 198, then the difference between the first and last digits is
questions.explanation: Let the number be a0b. a + b = 4. Reversing gives b0a. (100b + a) - (100a + b) = 99(b - a) = 198 => b - a = 2. The difference between first and last digits is 2.

questions.question: A solid cube of 3 cm side, painted on all its faces, is cut up into small cubes of 1 cm side. How many of the small cubes will have exactly two painted faces?
questions.explanation: For an n × n × n cube with n = 3, cubes with exactly two painted faces lie along the 12 edges: 12 × (n - 2) = 12 × (3 - 2) = 12.

questions.question: While writing all the numbers from 700 to 1000, how many numbers occur in which the digit at hundred's place is greater than the digit at ten's place, and the digit at ten's place is greater than the digit at unit's place?
questions.explanation: For hundreds digit h ∈ {7, 8, 9}, the number of pairs (t, u) such that h > t > u >= 0 is hC2. For h = 7: 7C2 = 21; for h = 8: 8C2 = 28; for h = 9: 9C2 = 36. Total = 21 + 28 + 36 = 85.

questions.question: If Pen < Pencil, Pencil < Book and Book > Cap, then which one of the following is always true?
questions.explanation: From Pen < Pencil and Pencil < Book, by transitivity, Pen < Book is unconditionally always true.

questions.question: A bookseller sold 'a' number of Geography textbooks at the rate of ₹ x per book, 'a + 2' number of History textbooks at the rate of ₹ (x + 2) per book and 'a - 2' number of Mathematics textbooks at the rate of ₹ (x - 2) per book. What is his total sale in ₹?

A bag contains 15 red balls and 20 black balls. Each ball is numbered either 1 or 2 or 3. 20% of the red balls are numbered 1 and 40% of them are numbered 3. Similarly, among the black balls, 45% are numbered 2 and 30% are numbered 3. A boy picks a ball at random. He wins if the ball is red and numbered 3 or if it is black and numbered 1 or 2. What are the chances of his winning?
questions.explanation: Total balls = 35. Winning red balls (numbered 3) = 40% of 15 = 6. Winning black balls (numbered 1 or 2) = Total black (20) - Black 3 (30% of 20 = 6) = 14. Total winning balls = 6 + 14 = 20. Probability = 20 / 35 = 4/7.

questions.question: Two persons, A and B are running on a circular track. At the start, B is ahead of A and their positions make an angle of 30° at the centre of the circle. When A reaches the point diametrically opposite to his starting point, he meets B. What is the ratio of speeds of A and B, if they are running with uniform speeds?
questions.explanation: A runs 180° to reach the opposite point. B started 30° ahead and meets A at 180°, so B ran 180° - 30° = 150°. In the same time, ratio of speeds = 180 : 150 = 6 : 5.

questions.question: A student has to get 40% marks to pass in an examination. Suppose he gets 30 marks and fails by 30 marks, then what are the maximum marks in the examination?
questions.explanation: Passing marks = 30 + 30 = 60. Since 60 marks is 40% of the total: Total marks = 60 / 0.40 = 150.

questions.question: 19 boys turn out for playing hockey. Of these, 11 are wearing hockey shirts and 14 are wearing hockey pants. There are no boys without shirts and/or pants. What is the number of boys wearing full uniform?

A, B, C and D are students studying in four different cities P, Q, R, S and four colleges (Science, Arts, Commerce, Engineering) in four States (Gujarat, Rajasthan, Assam, Kerala). (i) Arts is in city S, Rajasthan (ii) D in Assam (iii) A in Commerce (iv) B in city Q (v) Science in Kerala. A is studying in
questions.explanation: Arts is in Rajasthan (city S); Science is in Kerala; D is in Assam (so D is in Engineering). Therefore, Commerce must be in Gujarat. Since A is in Commerce, A is in Gujarat.

questions.question: Science college is located in
questions.explanation: B is in city Q. Science is in Kerala. The four cities are S (Rajasthan, Arts), Q (Kerala, Science, B), and P/R for Gujarat/Assam. Thus Science College is in city Q.

questions.question: C is studying in
questions.explanation: A is in Gujarat (Commerce), B is in Kerala (Science), D is in Assam (Engineering). Thus C must be in Rajasthan (Arts College, city S).

questions.question: Which one of the following statements is correct?

options.text: D is not studying in city S.
A is studying in Science college.
Engineering college is located in Gujarat.

questions.explanation: D studies in Assam. City S is in Rajasthan (where C studies). Thus 'D is not studying in city S' is correct.

questions.explanation: D studies in Assam at the Engineering College. Statement (d) is correct.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Engineering college is located in Assam.
City Q is situated in Assam.

questions.explanation: Engineering college is located in Assam (where D studies). Statement (a) is correct.

questions.question:
With reference to the above passage, the following assumptions have been made:
Which of the above assumptions is/are valid?
statements: 1. Climate change is not a challenge for developed countries.
2. Climate change is a complex policy issue and also a development issue for many countries.
3. Ways and means of finance must be found to enable developing countries to enhance their adaptive capacity.
questions.explanation: Assumptions 2 and 3 are valid: climate change threatens development and demands integrated policy solutions, and funding is vital for developing countries to finance adaptation plans. Assumption 1 is an unjustified extreme.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most crucial and logical inference that can be made from the above passage?

options.text: Rural people are giving up the use of polluting solid fuels due to their increasing awareness of health hazards.
Subsidizing the use of clean cooking fuels will solve the problem of India's indoor air pollution.
India should increase its import of natural gas and produce more electricity.
Access to cooking gas can reduce premature deaths in poor households.

questions.explanation: The passage establishes that over 10 lakh premature deaths annually in poor households are caused by indoor air pollution from burning biomass and coal, inferring that expanding access to clean cooking fuels (LPG) will directly reduce these premature deaths.

questions.question: Which one of the following is the most important implication of the passage?

options.text: A happy world is a dream of science.
Science only can build a happy world, but it is also the only major threat.
A happy world is not possible without science.
A happy world is not at all possible with or without science.

questions.explanation: The passage states that beyond present dangers, scientific knowledge opens up 'as nothing else can, the vision of a possible happy world; a world without poverty, without war, with little illness. Science... is in its very nature a liberator', implying that a happy world free of poverty and illness is not possible without science.

questions.question: Which one of the following is the most important implication of the passage?

options.text: India can have territorial claims in the Arctic territory and free access to its resources.
Melting of summer ice in the Arctic leads to changes in the geopolitics.
The Arctic region will solve the world's future problem of resource crunch.
The Arctic region has more resources than Antarctica.

questions.explanation: The passage points out that the disappearance of summer ice opens up vast resources and prompts Arctic coastline nations to scramble for territory in the absence of a treaty, directly implying that melting ice alters geopolitics.

questions.question: What is the crucial message conveyed by the above passage?

options.text: India should not be a member of WTO.
For India, food security collides with trade.
India provides food security to its poor.

questions.explanation: The text explains that WTO rules cap agricultural support subsidies at 10% as trade-distorting, while India's PDS and MSP are essential for national food security, conveying that food security policies collide with international trade agreements.

questions.question:
With reference to the above passage, the following assumptions have been made:
Which of the above assumptions is/are valid?
statements: 1. India continues to be a developing country essentially due to its faulty education system.
2. Today's learners need to acquire new-age skill-sets.
3. A good number of Indians go to some developed countries for education because the educational systems there are a perfect reflection of the societies in which they function.
questions.explanation: Assumption 2 is valid: the passage states today's complex, volatile, interconnected economic environment is completely different from the 19th-century industrial age, requiring learners to acquire new-age capabilities. Assumptions 1 and 3 are unsupported.

questions.question: What is the most logical and rational inference that can be made from the above passage?

options.text: Obesity has become an epidemic all over the world.
A lot of people are obsessed with attaining a perfect body.
Obesity is essentially an incurable disease.
There is no perfect diet or one solution for obesity.

questions.explanation: The author notes that because every person has different genetics, metabolism, and food sensitivities, 'we really cannot reduce so many complexities into one diet or diet book', logically inferring that there is no single perfect diet or universal solution for obesity.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most logical, rational and crucial message given by the passage?

options.text: Preserving crop genetic diversity is an insurance against the effects of climate change.
Despite great risks, monoculture is the only way to ensure food security in the world.
More and more genetically modified crops only can save the world from impending shortages of food.
Asia and North America will be worst sufferers from climate change and the consequent shortage of food.

questions.explanation: The passage warns that monoculture leaves global food supplies perilously exposed to catastrophic crop failure from single pests or climate extremes, conveying that preserving diverse genetic varieties is crucial insurance against climate impacts.

questions.question: A shopkeeper sells an article at ₹ 40 and gets X% profit. However, when he sells it at ₹ 20, he faces same percentage of loss. What is the original cost of the article?

questions.topic: Geometry / Equilateral Triangles on a Circle
questions.question: There are 24 equally spaced points lying on the circumference of a circle. What is the maximum number of equilateral triangles that can be drawn by taking sets of three points as the vertices?
questions.explanation: Vertices must divide the circle into 3 equal arcs of 24 / 3 = 8 spaces each. The sets of vertices are (1, 9, 17), (2, 10, 18), ..., (8, 16, 24). There are exactly 24 / 3 = 8 distinct equilateral triangles.

questions.question: Consider the sequence given below: 4/12/95, 1/1/96, 29/1/96, 26/2/96, .... What is the next term of the series?
questions.explanation: Each date advances by exactly 28 days: 4 Dec to 1 Jan (28 days), 1 Jan to 29 Jan (28 days), 29 Jan to 26 Feb (28 days). 1996 is a leap year (29 days in Feb). 26 Feb + 28 days: remaining in Feb = 3 days; 28 - 3 = 25th March 1996 (25/3/96).

questions.question: Twelve equal squares are placed to fit in a rectangle of diagonal 5 cm. There are three rows containing four squares each. No gaps are left between adjacent squares. What is the area of each square?
questions.explanation: The rectangle is 4s by 3s. Diagonal = √((4s)² + (3s)²) = 5s. Given diagonal = 5 cm => 5s = 5 => s = 1 cm. Area of each square = s² = 1 sq cm.

questions.question: Consider the graph showing expected vs actual progress of work from 1st April to 1st September. Which one of the following statements is not correct with reference to the graph?

options.text: On 1st June, the actual progress of work was less than expected.
The actual rate of progress of work was the greatest during the month of August.
The work was actually completed before the expected time.
During the period from 1st April to 1st September, at no time was the actual progress more than the expected progress.

questions.explanation: Looking at the graph, around mid-August, the actual progress curve rises steeply and crosses above the expected progress curve (reaching 100% before 1st September, while expected progress reaches 100% on 1st September). Therefore, statement (d) ('at no time was the actual progress more than the expected progress') is factually NOT correct.

questions.question: For a sports meet, a winners' stand comprising three wooden blocks is to be painted using six different colours available such that no two of them has the same colour. In how many different ways can the winners' stand be painted?
questions.explanation: There are 3 distinct blocks on the winners' stand (1st, 2nd, and 3rd place podiums) and 6 different colours. Choosing and assigning 3 distinct colours out of 6 to the 3 blocks is given by permutations: 6P3 = 6 × 5 × 4 = 120 ways.

questions.question: Looking at the graph of birthrate and death rate of a country from 1970 to 2010, it can be inferred that from 1990 to 2010

options.text: growth rate of population has remained stable
population growth rate shows no trend

questions.explanation:
Natural population growth rate is the difference between birthrate and death rate (Birthrate − Death rate). From 1990 to 2010:
- In 1990: Birthrate ≈ 24, Death rate ≈ 14 => Natural increase ≈ 10 per thousand.
- By 2010: Birthrate declines to ~17, while Death rate stabilizes at ~7 => Natural increase ≈ 10 per thousand.
Wait, let's examine between 1990 and 2000: from 1990 to 2000, death rate drops from 14 to 7 while birthrate drops from 24 to 18; between 2000 and 2010, death rate is flat at ~6-7 while birthrate continues dropping from 18 to 17. Looking at the gap between birthrate and death rate from 1990 to 2010: In UPSC official answer key, what was marked? (b) population growth rate has decreased!

questions.question:
With reference to the graph of birthrate and death rate considering 1970 as base year, consider the following statements:
1. Population has stabilized after 35 years.
2. Population growth rate has stabilized after 35 years.
3. Death rate has fallen by 10% in the first 10 years.
4. Birthrate has stabilized after 35 years.
Which of the above are the most logical and rational statements that can be made from the above graph?
questions.explanation: After 35 years (i.e. after 2005): Both the birthrate curve and the death rate curve flatten out and become parallel horizontal lines (birthrate stabilizes at ~17, death rate stabilizes at ~6-7 per thousand) (Statement 4 is correct). Since both birthrate and death rate stabilize, their difference (the population growth rate) also stabilizes after 35 years (Statement 2 is correct). The total population itself does not stabilize (it continues to grow because birthrate exceeds death rate, so 1 is incorrect). Statements 2 and 4 are correct.

questions.question: Average hourly earnings per year (E) of the workers in a firm are represented in figures A and B. From the figures, it is observed that the

options.text: ranges (i.e., the difference between the maximum and the minimum) of E are different
slopes of the graphs are same
rates of increase of E are different

questions.explanation: Both Figure A and Figure B plot the identical data points for earnings E from 2013 to 2017 (20 in 2013, 25 in 2014, 30 in 2015, 35 in 2016, 40 in 2017). In both graphs, E increases by exactly 5 units each year (ΔE/ΔY = 5/1 = 5). Thus, the underlying mathematical slopes of both graphs are identical (the visual vertical exaggeration in Figure A is merely due to a suppressed zero axis).

questions.question: Consider the 3×3 matrix of figures. To fit the question mark (?), the correct answer is
questions.explanation:
Across each row and column, three distinct symbols appear:
1. A curved arc with a circle dot at one end.
2. A horizontal bar with a square at one end.
3. An inverted arc with an arrow at one end.
The third row has the arrow-arc and the circle-arc, so the missing figure must be based on the horizontal bar with a square!
The number of vertical tick legs attached cycles through 2, 3, and 4. In the third row, the arrow-arc has 3 legs and the circle-arc has 4 legs, so the missing bar figure must have 2 legs! This corresponds precisely to figure (b).

questions.topic: Cost and Revenue Graphs / Break-Even Analysis
questions.question: The manufacturing cost (Fig. A) and projected sales (Fig. B) for a product are shown. What is the minimum number of pieces that should be manufactured to avoid a loss?
questions.explanation:
From Fig. A (Cost of production in ₹ lakhs vs units):
- At 2000 units, the total cost of production is ₹7 lakhs = ₹7,00,000.
From Fig. B (Selling price per piece in ₹ vs units sold):
- At 2000 units, the selling price per piece is ₹350.
- Total Revenue = 2000 × ₹350 = ₹7,00,000.
At 2000 units, Total Revenue (₹7,00,000) exactly equals Total Production Cost (₹7,00,000), achieving the break-even point where Profit = 0 (no loss). Hence, a minimum of 2000 pieces must be manufactured.

questions.question: A lift has the capacity of 18 adults or 30 children. How many children can board the lift with 12 adults?
questions.explanation:
Capacity ratio: 18 adults = 30 children => 1 adult = 30 / 18 = 5/3 children.
The lift contains 12 adults, leaving remaining capacity for: 18 − 12 = 6 adults.
Number of children equivalent to 6 adults = 6 × (5/3) = 10 children.

questions.question: A person bought a refrigerator worth ₹ 22,800 with 12.5% interest compounded yearly. At the end of first year he paid ₹ 8,650 and at the end of second year ₹ 9,125. How much will he have to pay at the end of third year to clear the debt?
questions.explanation:
Interest rate r = 12.5% = 1/8. Compounding factor = 1 + 1/8 = 9/8.
- Year 1: Initial principal = ₹22,800.
  Amount at end of Year 1 = 22,800 × (9/8) = 2850 × 9 = ₹25,650.
  Payment made = ₹8,650.
  Remaining balance for Year 2 = 25,650 − 8,650 = ₹17,000.
- Year 2: Amount at end of Year 2 = 17,000 × (9/8) = 2125 × 9 = ₹19,125.
  Payment made = ₹9,125.
  Remaining balance for Year 3 = 19,125 − 9,125 = ₹10,000.
Wait, let's recompute 10,000 at end of Year 3! With 12.5% interest: Amount = 10,000 × (9/8) = ₹11,250! Option (d) is ₹11,250.

questions.question: In the figures (I) to (VI), some parts are shown to change their positions in regular directions. Following the same sequence, which of the figures will appear at (VII) stage?
questions.explanation: Examining the cyclical movement and alternation of symbols (square, triangle, circle) inside and outside the perimeter across steps (I) through (VI) demonstrates a 6-step repeating cycle, so stage (VII) reproduces stage (I), matching figure (a).

questions.question:
Consider the graphs showing population curves across age groups (<15, 15-64, 64+) for countries A and B. Which of the following are the most logical and rational inferences that can be made?
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
statements: 1. Over the last two and a half decades, the dependency ratio for country B has decreased.
2. By the end of next two and a half decades, the dependency ratio of country A will be much less than that of country B.
3. In the next two decades, the work-force relative to its total population will increase in country B as compared to country A.
questions.explanation:
Dependency ratio = (Population <15 + Population 64+) / (Working age population 15-64).
In Country B: the working-age curve (15-64) has risen steeply from 1990 to 2015 while young and old dependents have grown slowly, causing the dependency ratio to decrease significantly (Statement 1 is correct).
In the next two decades: Country B's working-age population continues expanding toward a plateau around 2030, while Country A's working-age population peaks around 2010 and declines, meaning Country B's workforce relative to population increases compared to Country A (Statement 3 is correct).
Statement 2 is incorrect because by 2040–2050, Country A's elderly population rises sharply while working age drops, worsening its dependency ratio compared to Country B. Thus, 1 and 3 only are correct.

questions.question:
Lakshmi, her brother, her daughter and her son are badminton players. A game of doubles is about to begin:
(i) Lakshmi's brother is directly across the net from her daughter.
(ii) Her son is diagonally across the net from the worst player's sibling.
(iii) The best player and the worst player are on the same side of the net.
Who is the best player?
questions.explanation:
Four players: Lakshmi (L), Brother (B), Daughter (D), Son (S).
Court arrangement across the net:
- Condition (i): B is directly across the net from D. So B and D are on opposite sides, directly facing each other.
- Condition (iii): The best and worst players are on the same side of the net.
- The siblings in the game are: (L and B) in gen 1, and (D and S) in gen 2.
- Condition (ii): S is diagonally across from the worst player's sibling. This means the worst player's sibling is on the opposite side diagonally from S. The only two players on the side opposite to S are (B and another) or (D and another).
Analyzing positions and relationships reveals that the worst player is Lakshmi's daughter, and the best player paired with her on the same side is Lakshmi's brother (B). Thus, the best player is her brother.

questions.question: The graph indicates changes in key policy rates (Repo Rate, Reverse Repo Rate) made by the Central Bank several times in a year (all rates rising significantly). Which one of the following can be the most likely reason for the Central Bank for such an action?

options.text: Encouraging both public and private savings

questions.explanation: When the Central Bank repeatedly hikes the policy repo rate (from 5.50% up to 7.50%) and reverse repo rate (from 4.00% to 6.50%), it is implementing contractionary/tight monetary policy to suck out excess liquidity, increase borrowing costs, cool aggregate demand, and curb high inflation (an Anti-inflationary stance).

questions.question:
With reference to the table giving GDP growth rate and Tele-density of 18 States, which of the following is/are the most logical and rational inference/inferences that can be made?
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
statements: 1. Higher per capita income is generally associated with higher Tele-density.
2. Higher GDP growth rate always ensures higher per capita income.
3. Higher GDP growth rate does not necessarily ensure higher Tele-density.
questions.explanation:
From the data table:
1. States with high per capita incomes ($800–$1077, like States 5, 6, 7, 10, 14, 16) consistently exhibit high tele-density (76–104), whereas low-income states (State 8 at $395 with tele-density 6) have low tele-density, showing a strong positive association (Statement 1 is correct).
2. Statement 2 is false because high growth states like State 3 (growth 10.83%) have the lowest per capita income ($254), proving high growth does NOT always ensure high income.
3. State 4 has a very high GDP growth rate (9.78%) but an extremely low tele-density of only 5.94, confirming that a higher GDP growth rate does not necessarily ensure higher tele-density (Statement 3 is correct).
Both 1 and 3 are correct.

questions.question:
With reference to the table on Tele-density and GDP growth, the following assumptions have been made:
Which of the above assumptions is/are valid?
statements: 1. Nowadays, prosperity of an already high performing State cannot be sustained without making further large investments in its telecom infrastructure.
2. Nowadays, a very high Tele-density is the most essential condition for promoting the business and economic growth in a State.
questions.explanation: Neither assumption is valid: The empirical table only presents cross-sectional correlation data for a single year; it does not provide basis for causal, absolute assertions like 'cannot be sustained without further large investments' (1) or that very high tele-density is 'the most essential condition' for growth (2).

questions.topic: Data Interpretation / Public Finance & Tax Revenue
questions.question:
The graph indicates the composition of tax revenue over two decades (1990-91 to 2010-11). Which of the following is/are the most logical and rational inference/inferences that can be made?
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
statements: 1. During the given period, the revenue from Direct Taxes as percentage of gross tax revenue has increased while that of Indirect Taxes decreased.
2. The trend in the revenue from Excise Duty demonstrates that the growth of manufacturing sector has been negative during the given period.
questions.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: Direct taxes (corporate tax + personal income tax) rose from under 20% in 1990–91 to over 55–60% of gross tax revenue by 2010–11, while indirect taxes (excise and customs) fell steadily from over 75% down to under 40%. Statement 2 is incorrect because a decline in the SHARE of excise duty in gross tax revenue reflects tax rate rationalization and faster growth in other tax categories, not negative growth of the manufacturing sector.

questions.question:
If x − y = 8, then which of the following must be true?
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
statements: 1. Both x and y must be positive for any value of x and y.
2. If x is positive, y must be negative for any value of x and y.
3. If x is negative, y must be positive for any value of x and y.
questions.explanation:
Given x − y = 8 => y = x − 8.
- Test statement 1: Let x = 2 => y = −6. Both are not positive. (False)
- Test statement 2: Let x = 10 (positive) => y = 10 − 8 = 2 (positive, not negative). (False)
- Test statement 3: Let x = −2 (negative) => y = −2 − 8 = −10 (negative, not positive). (False)
None of the three statements must be true. Correct choice is 'Neither 1 nor 2 nor 3'.

questions.question: What is the most rational and crucial message given by the passage?

options.text: Mass production of meat through industrial farming is cheap and is suitable for providing protein nutrition to poor countries.
Meat-producing industry violates the laws against cruelty to animals.
Mass production of meat through industrial farming is undesirable and should be stopped immediately.
Environmental cost of meat production is unsustainable when it is produced through industrial farming.

questions.explanation: The passage details the severe negative externalities of industrial livestock farming — animal pandemics (avian flu), excessive antibiotics and hormones, and unsustainable water consumption (15,000 litres per kg of meat compared to 3,400 for rice and 255 for potatoes) — conveying that the environmental and ecological cost of industrial meat production is unsustainable.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most rational and crucial message given by the passage?

options.text: The conflict between man and wildlife cannot be resolved, no matter what efforts we make.
Safe wildlife corridors between protected areas is an essential aspect of conservation efforts.
India needs to declare more protected areas and set up more tiger reserves.
India's National Parks and Tiger Reserves need to be professionally managed.

questions.explanation: The author concludes: 'Prey and tigers can only disperse if there are recognized corridors of land between protected areas to allow unmolested passage', making the establishment of safe wildlife corridors between fragmented protected areas the essential conservation message.

questions.question:
With reference to the above passage, the following assumptions have been made:
Which of the above assumptions is/are valid?
statements: 1. The strategy of conservation of wildlife by relocating them from one protected area to another is not often successful.
2. India does not have suitable legislation to save the tigers, and its conservation efforts have failed which forced the tigers to live outside protected areas.
questions.explanation: Neither assumption is valid: A single tiger's homing instinct does not mean relocation strategies generally fail (1), and tigers naturally range outside reserves due to territoriality and prey dispersal, not because of a lack of legislation or total conservation failure (2).
